13	The 0.56pp cross-model exception gap (Appendix~\ref{sec:robustness_analysis}) and the format-collapse nature of the DeepSeek outlier (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}) further support that the signal, not the model, is the binding constraint.

Three patterns emerge from the budget curve.
\emph{Phase transition at 256$\to$512 tokens}: all three models jump +14.7--23.0pp (Qwen-7B +14.7, DeepSeek +17.5, Qwen-1.5B +23.0), crossing from near-baseline to near-ceiling in a single budget doubling.
The threshold aligns with the typical exception traceback length (${\sim}$500 tokens): below this budget, the diagnostic event is truncated; above it, the event is captured regardless of model capacity or architecture.

\emph{Convergence at tail-512+}: once the phase transition is crossed, all three models converge into a narrow 93.6--95.6\% band at tail-512 and an even tighter 96.5--96.6\% band at tail-1024.
Scale and architecture differences that dominate the signal-poor regime (tail-256 range: 72.6--78.9\%, 6.3pp) vanish in the signal-rich regime (tail-1024 range: 96.5--96.6\%, 0.1pp).

\emph{Scale behavior inversion}: in the signal-poor regime (tail-256), smaller models perform worse (Qwen-1.5B 72.6\% vs.\ Qwen-7B 78.9\%, $-$6.3pp), mirroring the \texttt{no\_trace} scale pattern.
In the signal-rich regime (tail-512+), this reverses: Qwen-1.5B matches or exceeds Qwen-7B (95.6\% vs.\ 93.6\% at tail-512; 97.9\% vs.\ 97.3\% at tail-2048), confirming that sufficient trace signal eliminates the capacity advantage.

\emph{Non-monotonicity}: DeepSeek-6.7B shows a $-$1.5pp decrease from tail-1024 (96.5\%) to tail-2048 (95.0\%), while the other two models increase monotonically.
This architecture-specific sensitivity is consistent with DeepSeek's known vulnerability to long-context formatting (Appendix~\ref{sec:training_dynamics}): additional tokens beyond the diagnostic window introduce noise that this model cannot filter as effectively.

Table~\ref{tab:head_vs_tail} confirms the truncation direction effect across all models: tail-2048 outperforms head-2048 by 15.5--22.6pp.
The gap is largest for Qwen-1.5B (+22.6pp), indicating that smaller models benefit most from positional proximity to the diagnostic signal, as they lack the capacity to locate it within longer, noisier prefixes.

\paragraph{Tokenizer efficiency and training dynamics.}
CodeLlama's tokenizer produces ${\sim}$20\% more tokens than Qwen's on identical trace inputs (mean 1{,}174 vs.\ 978 tokens), reducing the verdict label's share of the training loss to ${\sim}$0.085\%.
Under standard next-token loss, the model allocates the vast majority of gradient updates to predicting trace tokens rather than learning the verdict classification boundary.
This tokenizer-driven dilution is invisible at short trace budgets (tail-256/512), where CodeLlama performs comparably to other models (77.9\% and 97.5\%, respectively), but is expected to compound at longer budgets (1{,}024+ tokens) where trace tokens dominate the loss landscape.
A label-only loss variant (computing loss only on the verdict token, masking all trace positions) addresses this by decoupling verdict learning from trace prediction; results for CodeLlama tail-1024/2048 under this regime are pending.
This finding highlights tokenizer efficiency as a previously overlooked variable in trace-based training: architectures with less efficient tokenizers require adapted training strategies (e.g., label-only loss) to prevent the diagnostic signal from being drowned by trace token prediction.

\begin{abstract}
Execution traces are increasingly used to enhance code language models, but which trace components matter for downstream tasks remains poorly understood.
We present the first systematic component ablation of trace representations for verdict prediction (classifying whether a test passes or fails) across four models spanning three architecture families and 1.5B to 13B parameters.
Exception events alone achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% accuracy across all four models (${\geq}$99.83\% on three of four; one seed reaches 100\%), while a code-only baseline shows 9.19pp scale sensitivity (67.3--76.5\%).
Adding more trace information actively hurts: a multi-component representation underperforms exception-only, and the full-trace gap approximately decomposes into information overload (${\sim}$74\%) and gradient dilution (${\sim}$26\%).
Tail-truncation experiments reveal that diagnostic signal concentrates near the trace terminus (in a localized window, not the absolute end), recovering 86\% of the gap to exception-only.
A format-marker ablation confirms ${\sim}$91\% of the exception signal is semantic (learned by SFT to distinguish caught from uncaught exceptions) rather than format-driven.
These results reveal a two-tier diagnostic hierarchy: Tier~1 signals (exception events, assertion points) individually achieve ${\geq}$99\%, while Tier~2 (loop compression) reaches 85.6\%.
Cross-dataset evaluation on DebugBench ($N{=}426$) confirms generalization, with exception-only achieving 100\%.
We reframe verdict prediction as fault detection: the minimal sufficient signal is a compact exception event (median 150 tokens) that is scale-invariant, architecture-independent, and deployable in token-constrained settings.
\end{abstract}
